title: Sweet is your will
hookLine: a line about sweetness that Sikh tradition ties to Guru Arjan's death in Lahore, and to accepting God's will (Guru Granth Sahib 394)

lines: A LINE FOR A GOOD DAY?
SIKH MEMORY TIES IT TO LAHORE.
cards: Tera kiya meetha laagai. Sikhs sing this line, and it means, roughly: what you do tastes sweet to me. On paper it sounds like a line for a good day: a wedding, a new baby, a harvest in.
But Sikh memory ties it to Guru Arjan, one of the Sikh Gurus, and to the end of his life.
Tradition says he was arrested and held in Lahore, tortured there, and died, and that this was the line he lived inside while it happened.

teach.b: First, the line itself. It sits on page 394 of the Guru Granth Sahib, in a hymn by Guru Arjan, and runs, in paraphrase: your doing seems sweet to me; Nanak asks for the treasure of the Name.

Nanak there is a signature: the later Gurus sign their hymns with the first Guru's name. It doesn't say what you do is easy, or fair, or what I'd have chosen. Meetha is a taste word, sweet in the mouth.
And the hymn asks for one thing back: not a way out, the Name. Second, the story.

teach.h: THE HOT PLATE AND THE CALM.
teach.b: Sikh tradition tells that the Guru was made to sit on a hot iron plate while burning sand was poured over him. The accounts differ in their details, and historians weigh them.
What tradition holds onto most is not the cruelty but his calm. Third, the friend.

teach.h: A FRIEND OFFERS TO STEP IN.
teach.b: Tradition says the Sufi saint Mian Mir, a Muslim and a friend of the Guru, offered to step in and plead for him, and the Guru asked him not to. This too, he said, is the will.
Sikhs call that will bhana, what pleases God, and remember Guru Arjan as a picture of accepting it. Fourth, what it isn't. Accepting the will is not folding your hands or calling evil good.
The same tradition remembers his death as a wrong done to him, and honors him as a martyr.
And it holds acceptance right beside chardi kala, rising spirits, which this path met in its first year.
Acceptance here isn't defeat. It's refusing to let the pain decide who you are.

how: Sikhs sing tera kiya meetha laagai in kirtan, and they remember Guru Arjan's martyrdom with gatherings and with chhabeel, stalls that offer cool sweetened water to anyone passing by.

o: God's will, accepted without going bitter
a Sikh hymn sung only at weddings and births
giving up and letting others decide

games.q: inside the sweet line — tap the pairs.
p: where the line sits in the Guru Granth Sahib
a Sufi friend who offered to step in

s: in the hymn, Nanak asks God for a way out of suffering
Guru Arjan, signing as Nanak, asks for the treasure of the Name, not an escape.
accepting the will, in Sikh teaching, means doing nothing
it sits beside chardi kala, rising spirits, and the tradition honors Guru Arjan as a martyr wronged.
tradition remembers Guru Arjan for his calm under torture
and for asking his friend Mian Mir not to step in.

games.q: you're Guru Arjan, held in Lahore. your friend Mian Mir, a Sufi saint, offers to step in and plead for you. what do you say?
o: help me find a way to escape.
don't: this too is the will.
games.why: tradition says the Guru asked his friend not to intervene and accepted what came. it's a story Sikhs tell; the details vary between accounts.

practice: Hold one thing you can't change, small enough for two minutes: a delay, a diagnosis, a choice someone else already made.
Breathe in and say inside, this is what is; breathe out and let one place that's pushing against it, the jaw, the shoulders, the stomach, stop pushing for a breath or two.
Nobody asks you to call it sweet; if you pray, hold the Guru's line, tera kiya meetha laagai, or simply, this is what is.

wordCard.voice: Bhana, the Sikh word for what pleases God, accepting what can't be changed without going bitter and without giving up. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi in Gurmukhi script: sweet. from the line ਤੇਰਾ ਕੀਆ ਮੀਠਾ ਲਾਗੈ, your doing seems sweet.

carryVoice: Your line: this too is the will. Here, acceptance sits right beside rising spirits. Until tomorrow.
